title: California Will Fine Robotaxi Operators Up to $10,000 Per Vehicle for Blocking First Responders
excerpt: Senate Bill 1246 requires local incident technicians, U.S.-based remote drivers and fleet-status alerts — with penalties starting July 2028.
body:
• Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 1246 this week, giving California cities and counties the power to fine robotaxi operators that block first responders.
  • A court can order up to $10,000 per vehicle when an autonomous vehicle obstructs an emergency operation for more than 30 minutes, plus up to $5,000 per violation of the law's dispatch rules.
  • Operators must dispatch local on-the-ground incident technicians after crashes or on a responder's request — and remote drivers who take direct control must be based in the United States with a California-valid license.
  • The rules take effect July 1, 2028; the California DMV must set response-time guidelines by the same date.

California has put a dollar figure on one of the robotaxi industry's most persistent failures. Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 1246 into law this week, authorising fines of up to $10,000 per vehicle when a driverless car obstructs police, firefighters or ambulances for more than half an hour — and requiring operators to put real people on the ground when things go wrong.

What the law demands

The legislation creates two civil penalties. A court can order up to $10,000 for each commercial autonomous vehicle that obstructs or interferes with an emergency for more than 30 minutes — with the clock starting from the moment an emergency official requests a local incident technician. A second penalty of up to $5,000 applies per violation of the dispatch rules. A city attorney or county counsel must bring the case, and the violation is civil, not criminal.

https://x.com/TheRideshareGuy/status/2106396931287052652

The operational requirements are at least as significant as the fines. Companies must dispatch a "local incident technician" immediately after a crash or when a first responder requests help — technicians who can actually relocate or tow the vehicle, not just advise by phone. For driverless vehicles without manual controls, remote staff must be able to put the car in neutral so officials can move it, or switch it off. And during a fleetwide failure, companies must immediately tell local jurisdictions where their vehicles are and what condition they are in.

Perhaps most consequentially for staffing models, remote drivers — defined as people who brake, steer or shift in real time — must work from inside the United States and hold a license valid in California. The rule effectively curbs global remote-operation setups for the highest-control roles.

Context: years of frozen cars and frustrated firefighters

The law is a direct response to a documented pattern. Waymo, the largest U.S. robotaxi operator with roughly 4,000 vehicles — about 1,200 of them in the Bay Area — has repeatedly drawn complaints for stalled cars blocking firehouse exits, stalling in front of ambulances on emergency calls, and even relying on first responders to manually move broken-down vehicles. A TechCrunch investigation earlier this year highlighted cases in which the company leaned on firefighters and police to reposition its cars, prompting the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to demand that AV developers find "solutions" to the obstruction problem.

San Francisco firefighters have logged dozens of internal reports on robotaxi interference since early 2025 alone. One February incident saw a Waymo perform a three-point turn on Sanchez Street, end up facing the sidewalk, and hold up a fire engine for 15 minutes, according to the SF Standard.

Industry response

Waymo welcomed amendments made to the legislation. "We are grateful for the amendments made to the bill, which ensure autonomous vehicle operators can still feasibly serve Californians," a company spokesperson told TechCrunch, reiterating its commitment to road safety. Zoox also signalled it would comply. The industry now has until July 2028 — when both the law and the DMV's response-time guidelines take effect — to build the on-the-ground infrastructure the bill demands.

What it means for residents

For Californians, the law means the next time a driverless car freezes in an intersection during a crisis, someone with keys, a tow hook and a local phone number is legally required to show up. Fines alone don't move cars — but the staffing mandates behind them might.

nri_angle: Robotaxi operators like Waymo employ thousands of engineers and operations staff across California, including many Indian engineers in the autonomous-vehicle sector — the new U.S.-based remote-driver rule reshapes how those fleets are staffed.
